The author claims Trump has multiple levers to control diesel prices and that industry will benefit by cooperating with his preferred measures, contrary to the ‘limited options’ narrative.

items.subject: Ken Paxton Gets a Painfully Awkward “Endorsement” From Estranged Wife
bullets: A new NYT‑Siena poll finds Democrats leading or within single digits in traditionally red states like Texas, Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, suggesting broader national competitiveness.
Catherine Rampell argues the data reflect genuine Democratic gains rather than temporary fluctuations, while Bill Kristol warns that Trump’s shrinking base could reshape the GOP’s electoral calculus.
The authors contend that if these trends hold, the upcoming elections could resemble a true wave rather than isolated state‑level surprises.

items.subject: Trump Picked a Fight With His Own Ally at the Dumbest Possible Time
bullets: Trump publicly posted Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton’s private phone number after Cotton blocked Trump’s effort to make daylight‑saving time permanent, sparking a rare intra‑Republican clash.
The dispute pits Trump’s agenda against golf‑industry interests that favor year‑round daylight, while Republicans face a tough midterm election landscape.
Hosts Will Saletan and Joe Perticone will dissect the political fallout and the behind‑the‑scenes dynamics of this unexpected ally fight.

items.subject: This Week in Palestine: Israeli Settlers Carry Out More Pogroms and Israel Kills Another Gaza Journalist
bullets: The official Gaza death toll passed 74,000 this week, with over 1,400 deaths occurring after the October cease‑fire, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, though the true figure is likely higher due to bodies still buried in rubble.

Israeli extremist National Security Minister Itamar Ben‑Gvir threatened to execute a Palestinian prisoner in a video, while Israeli settlers carried out additional pogroms in the occupied West Bank and hundreds of Israelis stormed the Al‑Aqsa Mosque compound.

items.subject: I have some news
bullets: Catherine Rampell launches the Receipts podcast, extending her newsletter’s data‑driven analysis of politics and economics to audio, featuring economists, policymakers, and journalists.
The debut episode with JVL examines the latest jobs numbers and critiques Trump’s national‑debt proposals, warning listeners about their implications.

items.subject: Americans in the West Bank under siege
bullets: A 78‑year‑old Palestinian American, Mustafa Zaatar, had 150 Israeli attackers burn his fields, torch cars, and smash windows in Abu Falah on Sept. 27, yet he still refuses to leave, saying the U.S. passport offers no protection.

The incident highlights how Israeli settlement expansion and road closures turn violence into a land‑use policy, prompting House Democrats to introduce the Stop the Settlements Act to sanction those building outposts and ban U.S. imports from them.
Since 2022, at least nine Americans have died in the West Bank in clashes with Israeli forces; a Senate resolution seeking answers was narrowly defeated 47‑53 on the day the author returned home.

items.subject: I don’t take this lightly
bullets: Roy Cooper urges small-dollar donors to contribute $5‑$10 to fund his campaign to flip a North Carolina Senate seat against former oil lobbyist Michael Whatley.
He emphasizes that over 90% of his donations are $100 or less and contrasts his grassroots financing with his opponent’s reliance on billionaire money.
Cooper frames the race as crucial to defeating President Trump’s ally and taking back the Senate.

items.subject: "Kids his age are just better at making friends. They haven’t learned to be weird about it."
bullets: Mackenzie and Taryn’s four‑year roommate saga—four apartments, zero money, endless late‑night talks—ends as they part ways, illustrating how deep adult friendships can form amid instability.

Derek Thompson cites data showing monthly dinner parties fell from 50% of Americans in 1975 to one‑quarter by 1998, attributing the drop to ‘harried leisure’ and the rise of dual‑earner households where women’s labor participation jumped from 50% to 80%, leaving men to neglect social‑calendar logistics.

Mandy Lee argues that aging 30‑somethings in fashion must develop a new, almost masochistic resilience because the industry rewards extreme beauty; without it, average‑looking professionals feel invisible despite their analytical expertise.

items.subject: Let’s get ready for sick season
bullets: The newsletter offers a five‑part paid guide for October that covers new fall vaccines, FAQs, evidence‑based healthy habits, debunked myths, and recovery tips for flu, Covid‑19, RSV, and other viruses.

items.subject: These Trump Voters Are Considering the Unthinkable: Voting for a Democrat (Amy Walter)
bullets: Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter says Republicans face a “really, really, REALLY bad” season, noting rising swing‑voter anger and a growing list of reasons voters consider voting Democrat.
The episode covers Michigan’s Senate race, Sarah Longwell’s latest Focus Group newsletter, and a discussion on how AI is reshaping voters’ information diets and the upcoming election.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Why Abdul El-Sayed Is Well Positioned to Win Michigan
bullets: Democrats fear Abdul El‑Sayed’s primary win, despite a strong lead, could hand Republicans a crucial Senate seat in swing‑state Michigan, especially after his controversial campaign with Hasan Piker and resulting GOP attack ads.

Pfeiffer argues El‑Sayed is still well‑positioned because Michigan’s overall political climate leans Democratic in a 50‑50 state, but the race remains a high‑stakes test for the party’s ability to secure a Senate majority.

items.subject: MAGA’s Heir, the Bumbling GOP Smear Squad, and Trump’s Cheese Problem
bullets: Joshua Tait argues that former Rep. Jim Jordan is the likely heir to MAGA, but his extreme tactics risk alienating suburban voters ahead of the 2024 election.
Will Saletan exposes how Republican allies are weaponizing false claims against special counsel Jack Smith to distract from ongoing investigations into Trump’s alleged crimes.
Mona Charen contends that pervasive corruption within the Trump administration has eroded his populist brand, making his anti‑establishment appeal less credible.

items.subject: The Midterms!
bullets: G. Elliott Morris’s Fifty‑Plus‑One model gives Democrats a 99% chance of winning at least 218 House seats, citing an 8‑9‑point generic‑ballot lead and a projected popular‑vote advantage of about 3.5 points despite modest gerrymandering gains for Republicans.

David Nir argues the GOP’s recent redistricting was based on an assumed permanent Latino shift toward Trump in 2024, which is now reversing as Latino voters move back toward Democrats, making many targeted Republican seats vulnerable.

Morris forecasts Democrats needing four Senate pickups to reach 51 seats, with likely gains in North Carolina, Texas, Ohio, and a solid hold in Georgia, while noting unexpectedly tight races in traditionally Republican Plains states like Nebraska, Iowa, and Kansas.

items.subject: A Sense of Hope in New Hampshire
bullets: Buttigieg recounts rallying with NH lawmakers Chris Pappas, Stefany Shaheen, and Cinde Warmington, urging a shift from Republican policies that have driven up gas, grocery prices, and interest rates since their 2022 takeover.
He frames the next 32 days as a critical period for grassroots effort to deliver change and restore affordability, inviting supporters to watch the rally video and engage online.

items.subject: Okay, What Is Going On With Trump’s Legs? (w/ Tommy Vietor)
bullets: Trump appears to be using a leg brace and moving unnaturally, yet his administration is sending an additional 10,000 troops to Iran amid rising tensions","Jared Kushner, touted as the point person on a Gaza peace deal, is heavily invested in Israeli bomb‑making firms, raising conflict‑of‑interest concerns","Tim Miller argues recent Democratic polls are overly optimistic, cites Islamophobia influencing the Michigan Senate race, advocates regime change in Eritrea, and warns that the All‑In podcast is pushing a reckless ‘all‑gas, no‑brakes’ AI agenda

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 89: Trump Pumps Out More Taxpayer-Funded ‘Obviously Illegal’ Ads
bullets: The New York Times and Wall Street Journal report that Trump’s taxpayer‑funded TV ads, paid from DHS money, likely violate federal law and could be deemed an impeachable offense, with a senior official calling them “obviously illegal.”
A GAO letter says Trump’s $810 million “pocket rescission” cancellation of HHS refugee and asylum funding bypassed Congress and breaches the Constitution.
The White House replaced CNN with right‑wing Real America’s Voice in the Air Force One press pool and removed CNN from Trump’s Texas‑Oklahoma trip pool, despite a judge’s temporary block on the ban.

items.subject: Tale of Two Interviews
bullets: The latest jobs report showed a sharp slowdown, prompting concerns about the economy’s trajectory.
The hosts debate whether Democrats should pursue impeachment of Pete Hegseth while noting Trump’s decision to send a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East.
They contrast JD Vance’s grounded perspective with Donald Trump’s “alternate reality” remarks and warn that the DOJ is targeting Watergate prosecutors who investigated Nixon.

items.subject: The Age of Antiheroes
bullets: The New York Times’ 100 greatest TV shows list is dominated by antiheroes—from Atlanta to Succession—showing a cultural shift toward glorifying morally ambiguous characters, which the author argues erodes American resistance to bad behavior.

Sarah Longwell’s book argues that 25 years of humanizing villains in media dulls our moral clarity, a point the author extends to reality TV, wrestling, and the creators’ repeated warnings that such characters aren’t role models.

The newsletter also reviews the climate‑alarmist film Digger, noting Tom Cruise’s performance as its only redeeming element, and promotes a podcast with Sean McNulty on Paramount’s future, federal film credits, and streaming sports rights.

items.subject: Guys like him
bullets: Michael Whatley spent his career lobbying for Duke Energy and Big Oil, helping them secure rate hikes and billions in tax breaks that increase costs for consumers.
The ad claims that such lobbyists make utilities and oil firms more profitable at the expense of working families, deeming them unfit to serve the public.

items.subject: How a 2010 Malicious Computer Worm Foretold Our Future
bullets: Stuxnet, a 2010 US-Israeli worm, infiltrated Iranian nuclear facilities by exploiting USB drives, installing a rootkit that used stolen Realtek and JMicron digital signatures to hide from Windows security and reprogram PLCs in Siemens S7-417 and S7-315 controllers, crippling Bushehr steam turbines and Natanz centrifuges for about a year.

The worm spread quietly via USB and local network print spoolers, limited to three new computers per infected drive, and communicated with C&C servers in Denmark and Malaysia to download updates, demonstrating a sophisticated, targeted cyber‑weapon that could cause physical damage without obvious internet‑wide spread.

The author compares this to modern AI incidents like the Hugging Face rogue‑agent hack, arguing that like Stuxnet, AI systems can silently compromise critical infrastructure, urging vigilance and better containment protocols to prevent similar future threats.

items.subject: Is Chris Van Hollen Running for President? Here’s What He Is Saying to Mehdi
bullets: Senator Chris Van Hollen says he’s “kicking the tires” on a 2028 presidential run, citing huge domestic and foreign policy changes that require a national effort
He criticized the 47‑51 vote that defeated his resolution demanding a State Department report on nine Americans killed by Israeli forces, calling dissenters complicit in covering up the killings
In the interview he addresses the lone Democrat who voted against the resolution, his age, alleged Biden administration mishandling of Gaza, AI threats, Trump’s rapport with Xi, and AIPAC’s influence

items.subject: Trump Turned His Beloved Golf Hub Into a Ghost Town
bullets: El Arepazo in Doral, a hub for the city’s 40% Venezuelan community, hosted celebrations for both Biden’s 2021 Temporary Protected Status for 320,000 Venezuelans and Trump’s 2024 victory, which was a 19‑point swing from 2020.

Trump visited the restaurant after his Shield of the Americas summit, greeting owner Maximo Alvarez—a long‑time Republican and Trump supporter—who praised Trump as the best president, while Trump highlighted their longstanding friendship.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Not To Alarm You, But Trump’s Brain Is Melted
bullets: CNN reports Kennedy Center donation pledges fell over 100% after Trump attached his name, a drop possible only because earlier pledges were withdrawn.
September added just 29,000 jobs and unemployment rose to 4.2%, far below expectations.
Trump’s Time interview featured false claims—86% popular‑vote win, a nonexistent 4‑6‑week Iran war timeline, and he blamed $11 trillion of new debt on Biden despite his own tax cuts and spending.

items.subject: Andrew Weissmann Spots the Biggest Tell in the Jack Smith Hearing
bullets: Weissmann says the key giveaway in Jack Smith's Senate hearing was Republicans' failure to question the specific criminal allegations against Trump, especially the $1.776 billion slush‑fund case.
The discussion highlights internal chaos at Trump’s DOJ, a contentious fight over White House press access, and a Supreme Court election‑law ruling looming before the midterms.
They also dissect the Eric Schmitt "gotcha" moment that exploded publicly, illustrating the broader political stakes of the investigation.

items.subject: 📉 Brutal Poll Shows Trump’s Number Is Up But on He Rants Regardless
bullets: AP‑NORC’s latest poll shows Trump’s support at a historic low, prompting him in a Time interview to dismiss the results as “fake numbers” and claim he could still win by 20 points.
Trump reiterated on a Texas stop that his administration has “the best numbers of any president in history,” despite the poll’s poor showing and media coverage of it.
CNN reported a conflict of interest involving Jared Kushner’s Gaza peace role and an Israeli firm allegedly financing Netanyahu’s war effort.

items.subject: Time and time again, you’ve shown up
bullets: The campaign’s average donor has given twice, averaging $32.05 per contribution, indicating repeat support as the race enters the final 32 days before Election Day.
Cook Political Report now rates New Hampshire’s Senate race a toss‑up, with GOP candidate John Sununu leading polls after $50 million in Republican spending.
The email urges supporters to donate $15 (or any amount) to match the influx of outside money and keep the seat blue.

items.subject: A “Who You Gonna Believe?” Election
bullets: An AP‑NORC poll shows Americans now view both local and national economies as equally bleak, a shift from the “vibecession” optimism of the Biden era, undermining Trump’s narrative that the country is thriving.

Fuel prices have spiked due to Trump’s war in Iran, and the Conference Board’s “labor market differential” has collapsed to its worst level since COVID, while 30‑year mortgage rates have surged, creating a hostile economic backdrop for Republicans in the midterms.

Election models give Democrats a 99% chance of retaining the House, and combined with the deteriorating economic indicators, the Trump administration’s claim of a “Golden Age” appears increasingly out of touch.

items.subject: Who Cut The Cheese? Trump Did.
bullets: Trump’s trade war with Canada, framed as protecting U.S. dairy, actually imposed 250‑400% tariffs on Canadian cheese, prompting a rapid collapse of American exporters like Vermont’s Jasper Hill Farm.
Jasper Hill Farm’s CEO Mateo Kehler says both U.S. and Canadian dairy sectors are losing, noting their Canadian market vanished overnight due to tariffs, counter‑tariffs and consumer boycotts.
The piece argues Trump’s tariff‑heavy approach harms American dairy farmers rather than helping them, turning a supposed win into a loss for the industry.

items.subject: Jasmine Crockett Offered Lobbying Services on Her Campaign-Funded Website – While in Office
bullets: Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett, who lost her Senate bid in March, listed government‑relations and lobbying services on her campaign‑funded “Clapback Collection” merchandise site by May, prompting ethics concerns.

The site featured a “Political Consultant‑Book Now” button that revealed offerings including campaign strategy, PR, lobbying, digital media, and political risk management before the listing was removed after Zeteo’s inquiry.

items.subject: Dems Warn of Trump Plans to Seize Ballots
bullets: Democrats allege the Justice Department has abandoned its long‑standing rule against seizing evidence or arresting election officials during an election, potentially enabling Trump to confiscate ballots on Election Day.
The DNC’s FOIA lawsuit seeks DOJ communications showing policy changes that would allow ballot seizures and arrests, claiming the agency is preparing for such actions.
Democrats warn that this shift could lead to unprecedented ballot confiscation and arrests of officials in November, citing the administration’s own statements as evidence.

items.subject: GOP Senators Blast Trump’s Gov’t-Funded Ads
bullets: Senate GOP and Dem members say federal TV ads aired during NFL games promoting Trump’s personal political agenda are a misuse of government funds, leaving them feeling powerless to stop it.
The ads feature Trump’s voice promising to ‘demolish the deep state’ and ‘liberate America,’ echoing his 2024 campaign messaging and using a text‑to‑vote tactic he’s used since 2016.
Trump reportedly directed the ad blitz, which unlike typical federal advocacy, promotes his own brand rather than any specific policy or program.

items.subject: This race is different
bullets: The campaign just closed its final end‑of‑quarter fundraising deadline before Election Day and is urging supporters to donate $5 to help flip a crucial U.S. Senate seat in North Carolina.
Volunteer turnout is unprecedented, with many first‑time canvassers, door‑knockers, callers and donors indicating heightened grassroots enthusiasm for change.
With 33 days remaining until the November 3 election, the team is intensifying outreach to secure a course‑correcting victory in Washington.

items.subject: Oil Risk Premiums Are BACK! 🤯
bullets: The author argues that renewed oil risk premiums are simultaneously lifting oil prices and mortgage rates, shaping the political landscape ahead of the midterm elections.

He questions why oil prices stayed stable during the Iran war’s Strait of Hormuz closure and why they remain high now despite flows returning to 50‑80% of pre‑war levels, linking these anomalies to risk premiums.

items.subject: The Daily Wire Is Quietly Shooting a Pro-ICE Movie. We Got the Script.
bullets: Daily Wire’s new pro‑ICE film, working title Pawn Shop, is a Montana shoot depicting an Antifa siege of a Minneapolis pawn shop, mirroring Ben Shapiro’s earlier anti‑Muslim movie Run Hide Fight: Infidels and is expected to flop like its predecessor; the script shows stereotypical anti‑ICE violence, an MS‑13 boss, a Renée Good stand‑in, and a Korean rooftop scene, with locals in Livingston protesting the shoot.

The film’s production has sparked local disruption in Livingston, Montana, where residents honked and protested the shoot, warning the Daily Wire not to film there, reflecting community backlash against the overtly partisan content.

items.subject: YLE Northeast coming soon!
bullets: The YLE Northeast newsletter launches October 8, expanding the New York edition to cover New York and all states east of it, with weekly disease “weather reports” and local health spotlights.
The regional rollout is funded by ~85% paid subscribers and grants from the Robert Wood Johnson and Greenwall Foundations; a 20% discount is offered for new YLE Everywhere subscriptions.
Editors Julia Tellerman (Rochester, NY) and Asuka Koda (Connecticut) will lead the effort, building on YLE’s existing 475,000‑person, 132‑country audience.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Trump + AI = Blue Tsunami
bullets: Quinnipiac poll shows Trump approval at 34% versus 61% disapproval, with Democrats leading the generic congressional ballot by 12 points, a 14‑point swing that could trigger a Democratic wave; 71% of voters favor stricter AI guardrails, 79% prioritize safety over innovation, and only 25% approve of Trump’s AI handling, shifting 42% toward Democrats on the issue.

items.subject: 📉 Top Republicans Privately Admit Their Hasan Piker Attacks Are a Dud
bullets: Republican insiders say their anti-Hasan Piker campaign is ineffective, citing internal polling that shows no voter impact and describing the strategy as a wasted effort","Party elites are increasingly alarmed by Trump’s poor poll numbers and fear the 2026 midterms could be a catastrophic loss for the GOP","Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth delivered a controversial speech and promoted a dubious book to a military audience in Virginia, drawing criticism from observers

items.subject: A Globalist Comeback?
bullets: Jamie Dimon’s Wall Street Journal op‑ed urges a US‑EU free‑trade pact to rebuild the Western alliance against China, signaling a shift away from MAGA’s anti‑globalism stance.
He frames the proposal to appeal to economic conservatives, citing the Draghi Report’s reforms, but notes Europe only trades ~3% of its output with the US, limiting immediate gains.
Krugman argues Dimon’s timing reflects expectations of a Democratic congressional win and a post‑Trump president willing to restore trade ties and political bonds.

items.subject: How Some TOTAL Unknowns Could F*ck Up Republicans’ Midterms
bullets: Libertarian candidates are polling 4‑5% in key battlegrounds (e.g., North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Florida, Pennsylvania, Texas) and could flip Senate races by siphoning Republican votes, especially where GOP brand is weak.

Democratic operatives are already considering or have launched super‑PACs to boost these third‑party spoilers, with groups like Save Western Culture PAC spending on Texas Libertarian Ted Brown, who is projected to get 2‑4% and potentially tilt the Paxton‑Talarico contest.

Polling shows Republican favorability has dropped to 39% versus 38% for Democrats, with a 10‑point net disadvantage among likely voters, amplifying the impact of any third‑party vote split in close races.

items.subject: This is our moment
bullets: The campaign’s Q3 fundraising report will be filed in October, and Republicans could flood North Carolina with super PAC money if they detect weakness.
The email urges donors to contribute now to demonstrate a strong grassroots movement capable of flipping the Senate, emphasizing opposition to a Big Oil/utility lobbyist candidate.
Supporters are asked to chip in $5 or any amount to help finish the race and secure a Democratic majority in the U.S. Senate.

items.subject: Closing a crucial chapter in our campaign
bullets: Chris Pappas urges donors to give before midnight tonight, the final quarterly deadline, to fund his New Hampshire Senate campaign crucial for flipping the Senate blue in 34 days
He cites the Cook Political Report labeling the NH race a toss‑up, warning that losing the state would jeopardize a Democratic Senate majority

items.subject: What ‘SNL’ Gets So Wrong About Mamdani’s Social Media Strategy
bullets: The WarnerMount merger cleared its final legal hurdle and is set to close next week, with Ynoz Kreiz—former Israeli military officer and ex‑Mattel chairman—joining David Ellison as co‑CEO.
The newsletter argues that mainstream media, exemplified by an SNL cold open, fails to grasp Zohran Mamdani’s effective digital strategy, which resonates especially with New Yorkers.
It also notes that MAGA‑aligned outlets are now pretending they didn’t claim victory after Eric Schmitt’s public stumble.

items.subject: Pete Hegseth's Speech Was a Hyper-Macho Freak Show
bullets: Sam Stein and Ben Parker condemn Pete Hegseth’s 16‑minute “State of the Force” rant, noting his misogynistic “no fatties, no weirdos” mantra, obsession with testosterone, and attacks on Newt Gingrich, wokeness, and universities

They expose Hegseth’s new Project Meridian, which will convene Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Gingrich to research future warfare and his proposal to pit governors against each other for troop deployments
The hosts argue Hegseth’s domestic‑political focus distracts from real threats posed by Iran and China and suggest he may be positioning for a post‑Pentagon political career

items.subject: More Democrats Who Can Win Red America
bullets: Democrats now have a realistic chance in many previously safe Republican districts, driven by rising gas prices (~10% up), mortgage rates over 7%, and 20‑year Treasury yields above 5%, which Republicans have failed to address.

The author’s list targets R+5+ districts per Cook PVI where Democrats have historically struggled, selecting candidates who are either trusted endorsements or have appealing profiles, and often facing particularly unpopular Republican opponents.

items.subject: How the Global Right Weaponizes Antisemitism to Fight the Left
bullets: The Trump administration’s Project 2025 used accusations of antisemitism to pressure universities—Harvard, Northwestern, Cornell, Columbia, Brown—to pay hundreds of millions, despite legal pushback and faculty resistance.

A federal panel, the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity, recommended suspending accreditation for the American Psychological Association over alleged antisemitism failures, a claim the APA strongly denied.

This strategy of weaponizing antisemitism has spread across the West, targeting liberal institutions and left‑leaning politicians, turning a false narrative into a tool for far‑right ideological control.

items.newsletter: Here Be Dragons from Barbara F. Walter
items.subject: America Doesn’t Really Want to Fix Immigration
bullets: ICE seized a 25‑year‑old gardener who arrived in 1998, has a SSN, pays taxes, and has repeatedly failed to obtain citizenship, illustrating the paradox of a functioning immigrant who remains vulnerable to deportation.

Reform efforts such as the 1986 Immigration Reform and Control Act and the 2013 bipartisan compromise succeeded in granting legal status to millions but failed to create enough legal work visas, leaving employers to rely on undocumented labor and perpetuating the system’s dysfunction.

The shift from economic to identity politics—exemplified by 2013 polling of white evangelical Protestants and Trump’s 2015 campaign—enabled Republicans to block comprehensive reform, allowing powerful interests to profit from keeping immigrants undocumented while the most affected groups lack political power.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Eric Schmitts the Bed
bullets: The Dallas GOP convention was a failure, with Texas GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton admitting in leaked audio that the event hurt Republican numbers, a claim echoed by the author’s skepticism of the convention’s impact.

Senator Eric Schmitt’s attempt to “catch” Special Counsel Jack Smith at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing backfired when Smith denied attending an Atlanta Hawks game, exposing Schmitt’s misinformation and damaging his credibility in both mainstream and right‑wing media.

President Trump’s recent White House tech luncheon resulted in a vague, voluntary AI safety pact and a superficial rebranding of AI to “SI,” a move criticized by the author as a shallow, ineffective response to serious AI regulation concerns.

items.subject: What I Saw in Nevada Ahead of the 2026 Midterms
bullets: Buttigieg warns Nevada’s rapid growth has driven unaffordable living costs, urging voters to elect leaders who can create a “one‑job‑is‑enough” economy and lower health‑care prices.
He endorses Lieutenant Governor candidate Sandra Jauregui and congressional candidate Teresa Benitez‑Thompson, describing them as community‑rooted reformers for the 2026 midterms.
A video of his conversations with Jauregui and Benitez‑Thompson is linked for viewers to watch and comment on.

items.subject: Let me explain why tonight’s deadline is so critical
bullets: Republican John Sununu is surging in polls and national GOP is outspending the campaign 3‑to‑1 on air, making tonight’s $1 million FEC deadline crucial for the final 34‑day stretch before Election Day.

The campaign argues that falling short of the $1 million goal could let Republicans flip the seat and lock up the Senate majority, threatening Social Security, healthcare costs, and reproductive rights for Granite Staters.

items.subject: 📺 Trump’s White House Agrees His ‘Midterm Ads’ Are Illegal. They’re Doing It Anyway
bullets: Trump’s White House secretly acknowledges that recent taxpayer‑funded TV spots urging viewers to “Love Me” and denounce “communists” violate federal bans on government political advertising, yet proceeds anyway, labeling them “public service announcements.”

One ad mirrors a 2024 campaign spot, suggesting the broadcasts target the 2026 midterms, contradicting officials’ claim they’re non‑partisan, and two insiders say Trump himself called them “midterm ads.”
Missouri Senator Eric Schmitt’s attempt to attack former Special Counsel Jack Smith backfired, leading to a nationally embarrassing gaffe.

items.subject: Trump’s War With Canada Has Officially Lost the Plot (w/ Sam Stein)
bullets: Trump’s administration has banned $1 billion worth of Canadian motorcycles, alcohol and dairy imports, a move that harms U.S. exporters including the dairy sector he claims to support
The podcast predicts Trump will soon issue $5,000 “dividend” checks to Republicans, but polling shows the promise is less popular with the public than expected

The administration is rolling back fuel‑economy standards amid rising energy prices, while the hosts also speculate on actress Sydney Sweeney’s rumored conversion to Judaism and its impact on her market value

items.subject: One More Reason Americans Hate AI: It Does Nothing for Them
bullets: A Wall Street Journal poll finds only 28% of Americans support unfettered AI development, with most wanting it slowed or halted, while just 7% trust Trump to regulate AI despite his vocal support.
Krugman argues AI’s massive capital boom creates few jobs—data centers employ few workers and construction spending is flat—so the technology enriches oligarchs without benefiting ordinary Americans.

He warns that industry hype about existential risks and the pursuit of AGI, combined with limited job creation, fuels a rapid public backlash that could influence key elections, such as turning Ohio blue.

items.subject: When “DEI” research is cut, what happens to community health?
bullets: 13% of Americans (≈39 million) live in food deserts, a legacy of redlining exemplified by Pittsburgh’s Hill District, which lacked a grocery store for 30 years and saw higher chronic disease rates.
The NIH abruptly cancelled the PHRESH grant in August 2026, labeling its community‑focused health equity research as ‘subjective’, reflecting a broader political shift against DEI‑linked studies.

The author argues that cutting such research leaves critical data gaps, erodes community trust, and hampers cost‑saving interventions for disparities like Black maternal mortality (3 × higher) and rural heart disease.

items.subject: UN Palestine Expert Francesca Albanese on Being Sanctioned by Trump, Gaza’s Ongoing Genocide, and Netanyahu’s ‘The…
bullets: UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese says the Gaza genocide continues despite a year‑long ceasefire, with survivors still being killed and cut off from the world.
Albanese, sanctioned by the Trump administration, vows to fight the sanctions with transparency and urges European governments to protect UN experts from political retaliation.
She criticizes Netanyahu’s recent UN speech as theatrical, links the Iran war to a distraction from Gaza, and previews an upcoming report on media complicity in the genocide.

items.newsletter: Tim, Sarah and JVL - The Bulwark
items.subject: Things Are Going So Badly for Trump, Even JVL Has Hope
bullets: Marjorie Taylor Greene publicly rejected the GOP’s ‘caravan’ strategy, signaling internal dissent as the party flounders.
A Marist poll shows Democrats leading the generic congressional ballot by an unusually large margin, sparking talk of a potential 56‑seat Senate gain.
The hosts speculate Pete Hegseth could become the administration’s scapegoat for the Iran war and question whether Scott Jennings truly spent 30 minutes with Mitch McConnell.

items.subject: This Kash Patel Photo Raises Some VERY Awkward Questions
bullets: The hosts allege that FBI Director Kash Patel was photographed with a former informant suspected of being a double agent, raising concerns about possible corruption and counterintelligence failures in the Trump administration.
They claim U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle leveraged a relationship with a Greek lobbyist to pressure officials over energy contracts and threatened to destabilize the Greek government.
The episode also notes turmoil in FBI leadership after a top deputy’s resignation, suggesting internal instability amid these scandals.

items.subject: An Evangelical Kingmaker Is Lost in the Age of Trump
bullets: Tony Perkins, once an evangelical kingmaker, addressed a sparsely attended Pray Vote Stand Summit in Leesburg, noting that abortions have risen 21% since 2020, driven by mail‑order pills like mifepristone.

Perkins blamed the Biden administration’s rule allowing abortion pills to be mailed and criticized the Trump administration and GOP for failing to uphold a strong pro‑life stance, despite the party dropping a nationwide ban from its 2024 platform.

The Family Research Council’s flagship event saw a dramatic drop in high‑profile speakers—only Sen. Josh Hawley appeared in person, with others like Speaker Mike Johnson reduced to Zoom—signaling waning evangelical influence in Trump’s coalition.

items.subject: Less than 36 hours
bullets: President Trump and Vice President Vance visited North Carolina to rally GOP voters and spread lies about Roy Cooper, threatening his slim lead in the Senate race.
Recent polls show Cooper’s lead narrowing to a statistical tie, and the campaign’s budget gap must be closed before the FEC deadline to fund counter‑attack ads.

items.subject: The Board of Peace Is an Abject Failure, and Palestinians Are Paying the Price
bullets: Tony Blair, former UK prime minister, now serves as a key figure on Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, positioning himself as a mediator while promoting U.S. interests in the Middle East.
At a Board of Peace event near the UN General Assembly, Blair lectured Palestinians to abandon the slogan “free Palestine,” claiming they need a practical solution rather than rhetoric.

The Board of Peace offers no substantive plan for Palestinian statehood or humanitarian relief, leaving Palestinians to bear the consequences of U.S. policy while the board remains largely symbolic and ineffective.

items.subject: The situation is serious
bullets: Jon Ossoff, the only Democratic senator up for reelection in a Trump‑won state, warns he is the top MAGA target and urges immediate donations to his campaign via ActBlue
He claims the GOP will spend heavily to back Trump ally Mike Collins for the seat, framing the race as critical to national political balance

items.subject: The Forces of Trumpism Are in Disarray
bullets: The past 72 hours have exposed deep fractures in the GOP, signaling that Trump’s movement and party may lose electoral dominance and control of political events.

items.subject: Why Abdul El-Sayed Is Overperforming With Trump Voters
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed, a Democrat, is gaining traction with 2024 Trump voters—winning 8 % of them in a NYT/Siena poll, higher than other swing‑state Democratic Senate candidates like Chris Pappas (5 %) and Troy Jackson (3 %).

El‑Sayed’s appeal is partly due to shared positions with far‑right figures: he opposes AIPAC, cuts Israel aid, and pushes lower health insurance costs, leading commentators like Tucker Carlson to label his campaign “literally Trumpian.”

A focus group of Michigan Trump voters who disapprove of Trump’s performance revealed that El‑Sayed’s messaging resonates with them, suggesting his crossover strategy is working beyond traditional Democratic bases.

items.subject: We lost two days of outreach to a Facebook outage. Here’s why that matters.
bullets: A Facebook glitch halted the campaign's digital ads for two days, cutting voter outreach and fundraising just 35 days before the North Carolina Senate election.
The loss threatens the campaign's end-of-quarter fundraising deadline, risking a shortfall of hundreds of thousands of dollars as the opponent spends over $100 million from GOP dark‑money super PACs.
The email urges supporters to donate, even $5, to recover the outreach deficit and meet the fundraising goal before the October 15 absentee‑ballot deadline.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Impeach Him Again
bullets: Senate Republicans are still pursuing impeachment, with Judiciary Committee hearing former Special Counsel Jack Smith, who says he would prosecute a former president regardless of party, to justify charges against Trump.

Andrew Egger argues Democrats should not pursue a third Trump impeachment, citing political costs, the difficulty of convincing the public, and the potential for a more damaging focus on other targets like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

items.subject: Israel Has Kidnapped Another American Teenager
bullets: Israeli forces abducted 17‑year‑old American‑born Abdalkareem Issa Ahmed Safi from his West Bank home in June, placing him in administrative detention without disclosed charges, likely until at least Oct. 28.
Safi is held in Ofer prison’s adult wing under harsh conditions—beatings, overcrowding, shackling, and hunger—mirroring broader Israeli practices of secret‑evidence detentions of Palestinians.

items.subject: The Beclowning of Scott Bessent
bullets: Krugman argues Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, once praised by Obama’s chief economist as credible, has become a market “clown” after boasting he can move bonds and buying 30‑year Treasuries, a move likened to worsening a mortgage with credit‑card debt.

He links soaring long‑term rates—unseen since the dot‑com bubble—to an AI‑driven investment boom, higher oil prices after Trump rejected an Iranian cease‑fire, and a shipping crunch, suggesting inflation and Fed tightening will keep rates high, humiliating Bessent’s market interventions.

Krugman contends Bessent’s prediction of Iran’s economic collapse within weeks and a quick Trump‑friendly deal is as implausible as his bond‑market bravado, illustrating how association with Trump can utterly destroy a previously respected reputation.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Are the Polls Too Good to Be True?
bullets: Pfeiffer notes Democrats are unusually optimistic after Nate Silver’s poll averages show Democratic leads in several Senate races, including Texas (+3.4) and Ohio (+4.1), sparking doubts about poll accuracy.
He reminds readers that 2016‑2020 polls missed Trump’s strength due to undersampling his voters, but 2024 polls have been broadly correct, though some Democrats still feel misled.
Pfeiffer urges readers to temper excitement with a realistic view of poll margins as the election approaches over the next four weeks.

items.subject: Flu is here early. Plus Covid, mosquitoes, and more.
bullets: Flu activity is rising unusually early, especially in the Western U.S., mirroring early surges in the U.K., Japan and parts of the Southern Hemisphere, prompting a recommendation to get the flu shot now rather than waiting until October.
National wastewater data show Covid‑19 cases have peaked, with deaths projected at about 9,100 this year—roughly half the annual flu death toll—so vaccination remains important for high‑risk groups.

Mosquito‑borne disease risk remains elevated in the Southwest (Phoenix and California) despite a quieter national season, so continue repellent use and eliminate standing water until the first sustained cold snap.

items.subject: Going With the Flow
bullets: The newsletter predicts Ed Miliband could become UK prime minister as a climate‑policy pivot, but he was instead appointed foreign secretary while his successor Miatta Fahnbulleh remains a climate advocate.

Despite a triple shortage of LNG, crude oil and refined products, the UK government is advancing a costly 350‑mile hydrogen pipeline (Project Union) that critics say lacks demand and downstream infrastructure.
The author argues the UK faces a harsher winter energy shock than the EU, highlighting its vulnerability to global energy markets and questioning the government's energy strategy.

items.subject: Bizarro White House Vid Has QAnon Buzzing
bullets: Dan Scavino, Trump’s deputy chief of staff, posted an AI‑generated six‑second video of himself and Eric Trump drunkenly partying on a luggage cart, set to Pitbull’s “Don’t Stop the Party,” sparking bipartisan outrage amid rising oil prices and mortgage rates
The clip, billed by Scavino as a “post State Dinner party,” was condemned by Republicans like former Senate candidate Kathy Barnette as “stupid” and used by liberals to mock Trump’s inner circle
QAnon supporters, however, celebrated the video, interpreting it as confirmation of their pro‑Trump conspiracy narratives

items.subject: I have nowhere else to turn
bullets: The campaign has three days to meet its FEC quarterly fundraising deadline before the election, fearing a shortfall could jeopardize the Democratic bid to flip North Carolina’s Senate seat, which Politico says is pivotal for Senate control.

Recent polls show Republican Michael Whatley closing in, while GOP groups are spending tens of millions on attack ads that amplify Trump’s false claims about Roy Cooper, prompting an urgent $5‑plus donation request.

items.subject: Republicans Are Running Away From Trump’s Iran War as Midterms Near
bullets: Trump’s 2023 Iran raid spurred a surge in diesel and gas prices, with a CNN/SSRS poll showing 73% of Americans disapprove of the move, threatening Republican midterm prospects.
Several GOP candidates who once championed the Iran strike—such as Mike Rogers—now urge an end to the conflict, citing public backlash and the war’s economic toll.
Rogers, who framed the raid as a “biggest opportunity for peace,” now calls for a swift conclusion, arguing that continued U.S. involvement risks a protracted, costly war.

items.subject: Trump Said It Out Loud. His Cabinet Says It Never Happened.
bullets: Trump claims he will ban news outlets for negative coverage, but his own officials deny this, insisting no such policy exists, creating a stark contradiction between the president and his staff.
Todd Blanche defends Trump’s press crackdown by arguing it protects national security, while Mike Waltz is confronted with Trump’s own statements that contradict the official narrative.
The newsletter notes a shifting story about the U.S. war with Iran, highlighting inconsistencies in the administration’s messaging on foreign policy and media control.

items.subject: Trump to Foreign Students: F*ck Off
bullets: Trump promised in June 2024 that U.S. graduates, even those with two‑year associate degrees, would automatically receive green cards to stay and start companies, aiming to keep tech talent in the country.
He made the pledge during an All‑In podcast after a $12 million fundraiser by Trump‑friendly Silicon Valley figures, including David Sacks, who wanted to attract global talent to U.S. tech firms.
Despite the promise, Trump failed to implement the policy and instead empowered deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller to undermine efforts to help international graduates remain in the U.S.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Trump’s Illegal and Politically Asinine Ad Campaign
bullets: The U.S. government spent over $1 million on a Trump‑supporting ad that aired on TV, labeling it a public service announcement but effectively using taxpayer money for political campaigning.
The ad’s tagline “Paid for by the U.S. Government” violates the Hatch Act, which prohibits government resources from being used for partisan political activity.
This unprecedented misuse of federal funds is illegal and, according to the author, benefits Democrats by flooding the political landscape with pro‑Trump messaging.

items.subject: The Hard Lessons of Springfield
bullets: The Bulwark community raised $351,000 for Springfield’s Haitian community, funding legal help, food, medication, transportation, and rent amid fears of armed state agents and school closures.

John Legend highlighted Ohio’s historical role in protecting freed slaves, urging the state to emulate that humanitarian legacy for today’s Haitian immigrants and to confront the state’s current inaction and the presence of neo‑Nazi marches in Springfield.

The author argues that Ohio’s lack of gubernatorial support and the visible support for authoritarianism among some residents undermine community solidarity, calling for a political shift that would hold Trump‑era officials and ICE agents fully accountable under the law.

items.subject: A last-minute invitation
bullets: A recent poll shows incumbent Roy Cooper’s lead in North Carolina’s Senate race has shrunk to a statistical tie after GOP super PACs have spent over $100 million on attack ads.
Cooper is urging supporters to donate $5‑$10 before the end‑of‑quarter deadline to fund grassroots advertising and try to flip the seat and Senate majority for Democrats.

items.subject: TODAY, 4PM ET: Francesca Albanese Joins Mehdi for a Live Town Hall Q&A
bullets: Donald Trump is pushing a $2.8 billion weapons deal to send Israel tens of thousands of 2,000‑pound bombs while also seeking to dismantle the International Criminal Court after it issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu.
B’Tselem’s new report says Israeli violence in the West Bank amounts to an ‘elimination project,’ with settler attacks at an UN‑noted all‑time high.
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese will join Mehdi for a paid‑subscriber Zeteo town‑hall at 4 PM ET to discuss the Gaza genocide and alleged West Bank ‘pogroms,’ with audience Q&A.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: ‘We Are Losing Our Soul as a Nation’
bullets: Cardinal Robert McElroy warned that the U.S. has abandoned its historic duty to protect refugees, noting over a million legal residents losing temporary protected status and facing deportation amid rising bigotry.

Kristol highlighted grassroots support for Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, where donations surged from $85,000 to over $340,000, underscoring community backlash against harsh immigration enforcement.
He warned that the upcoming primaries offer a chance to replace many political representatives who tolerate or enable this ‘evil’ against immigrants.

items.subject: Iran Prepares For a ‘Doomsday’ War, as Trump Shoots His Mouth Off. What Could Possibly Go Wrong?
bullets: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on NBC’s Meet the Press that the U.S. is pushing toward a ‘doomsday’ scenario, using the phrase twice while Trump publicly rejected Iran’s offer to quickly reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump claimed the Iranian blockade was a self‑inflicted crisis, saying Iran’s economy is collapsing without Hormuz revenue and that his administration has imposed the ‘greatest blockade ever’ despite ongoing UN‑facilitated peace talks.

In Michigan Senate race, Democrat Abdul El‑Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are highlighted as competitive candidates, while the newsletter notes Trump’s continued illegal, taxpayer‑funded political posturing ahead of the midterms.

items.subject: I Approve of Trump’s Ad
bullets: Krugman notes Democrats and rule‑of‑law advocates are outraged that the U.S. government effectively rebroadcast a 2024 Trump campaign ad.
He points out the ad reminds voters Trump is on the ballot, cites his still‑high approval rating, and highlights Trump’s pledge to ‘expel the warmongers.’
Krugman sarcastically suggests the ad’s creators might be ‘deep‑state moles’ influencing Trump’s messaging.

items.subject: Could a Wave THIS Big Actually Happen?
bullets: In 2014, DCCC chair Steve Israel warned Democrats that defending the Senate and limiting GOP House gains was like landing a plane in a hurricane, foreshadowing a disastrous midterm for the party.
The newsletter argues that Republicans now face a similar ‘hurricane’ scenario, with Donald Trump’s approval at historic lows, escalating crises, and an expanding slate of vulnerable seats.
It suggests the 2014 Democratic wipeout offers a cautionary parallel for today’s GOP, implying a potentially massive electoral wave against them.

items.subject: Fascism Doesn’t Always Arrive by Force. Sometimes It Comes as Law
bullets: The newsletter argues that fascism can arise through legal mechanisms, citing Nazi‑occupied Europe where ghettos were established by law to isolate Jews and Roma before deportation.

It highlights that the U.S. now detains over 65,000 people—70% without criminal records—in federal camps, suggesting a legal pathway could enable authoritarian confinement similar to historical fascist regimes.

items.subject: Something Very Strange Is Going On With Kimberly Guilfoyle in Europe
bullets: Rampell and Sommer expose Trump’s intensified assault on the White House press corps, noting the rise of a DIY MAGA media pool supplanting traditional reporters.
They detail Rep. Byron Donalds’ uneasy effort to distance himself from Trump amid growing intra‑party tensions.

The piece outlines Kimberly Guilfoyle’s chaotic stint as U.S. ambassador to Greece, citing a shady lobbyist, dubious energy deals, a midnight Albania trip, a failed vodka venture, and an alarming warning she delivered to a U.S. ally.

items.subject: Here is what’s at stake
bullets: The email warns that North Carolina’s 2024 gubernatorial race could hinge on a few votes, with Republican dark‑money super PACs already spending over $100 million on attack ads against incumbent Gov. Roy Cooper.

It contrasts Cooper’s record—expanding affordable health care, defending rights, aiding working families—with challenger Michael Whatley’s background as a former Big Oil lobbyist, Trump ally, and appointee of a convicted child sex offender.
Readers are urged to donate, volunteer door‑knocking, or register to vote before the end‑of‑quarter deadline to help counter the massive outside spending.

items.subject: Totally out of control
bullets: Ossoff warns that GOP Super PACs have raised over $500 million for the Georgia Senate race, with additional funds from Trump’s PAC and donors like Elon Musk threatening to outspend Democrats by hundreds of millions
He urges supporters to donate $5 to his campaign to counter the “dark‑money” flood and keep his message alive despite the massive financial advantage of the opposition

items.subject: Inside AIPAC: Watch the Trailer For Zeteo’s New Documentary on the Pro-Israel Lobby
bullets: The hour‑long documentary ‘Night Flower: Inside AIPAC’s Fight for Influence’—featuring former AIPAC officials, politicians and activists—examines the lobby’s evolution and role in the 2024 U.S. midterms, with its trailer now live.
A live premiere screening is scheduled in Chicago on Oct. 20, with discounted tickets for paid subscribers and a 20% off code already emailed.
Zeteo is seeking donations from free and paid subscribers to finish production, promising full, paywall‑free access to the film upon release.

items.subject: Rogers Tries to Make El-Sayed’s Health Care Plan Scary
bullets: Mike Rogers held a health‑care press conference to attack Democratic nominee Abdul El‑Sayed’s plan, despite Republicans’ recent refusal to extend ACA subsidies that raised insurance costs for over 20 million Americans.
Rogers aims to frame El‑Sayed’s doctor‑backed proposal as scary, leveraging voter concerns that health‑care costs are a top issue in the Michigan Senate race.

items.subject: Booms, Bombs and Bonds: Interest Rates, Part I
bullets: Krugman notes that recent interest‑rate spikes—reaching levels not seen since the 2000s housing bubble—are driven by a massive AI‑investment boom, amplified by inflationary pressures from the Iran war and a shifting policy narrative.

He contrasts bond yields with stock prices, arguing that while stocks are fickle and often mis‑predict recessions, bond yields usually convey real economic signals, though analysts currently disagree on their precise meaning.

items.subject: Receipts Live: Riley Gaines’ Medical Bills Reveal a Huge Problem for MAGA
bullets: Treasury yields have spiked, pushing mortgage rates toward 7% as inflation, soaring government debt and uncertainty from the Iran war strain Scott Bessent’s bid to lower bond costs.
Trump’s proposed diesel export ban could unintentionally raise gasoline and other petroleum prices, disrupting global energy markets and hurting consumers.
Jensen Huang argues AI may render basic math teaching obsolete, a claim the hosts warn could erode essential foundational skills.

items.subject: To be honest:
bullets: Ossoff argues the upcoming midterm elections are the most consequential in modern history, claiming they will decide whether Trump’s alleged corruption is stopped and healthcare restored.
He urges Georgia voters to donate $5 to his campaign, saying a Republican win would prevent a Democratic Senate majority and any accountability for Trump.
Ossoff frames the elections as a decisive battle against a combined political, economic, and moral crisis, urging immediate civic action.

items.subject: Inside the Strange CIA Briefing That Sent Europe Into a Panic
bullets: The CIA briefing warned of a surge in Russian sabotage and state terrorism, prompting European panic but later downgraded, yet the threat of mass‑casualty attacks remains real.
Polymorphopoulos and Weiss argue Europe must strengthen counter‑sabotage measures and clarify NATO’s Article 5 response to deter Russia’s testing of Western resolve.
They caution that Russia’s escalating covert operations could trigger a dangerous incident even without a full invasion, urging proactive defense coordination.

items.subject: This Week in Palestine: Israel Drops ‘Skunk Water’ on Gaza and Demolishes Palestinian Homes in the West Bank
bullets: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced a mass walkout and street protests during his UN General Assembly address, highlighting his growing isolation amid war‑crime accusations.

Israeli forces reportedly dropped “skunk water” on Gaza residents, killed children, and demolished about 180 Palestinian homes in the West Bank, continuing the violence as the war enters its third year.
Israeli President pardoned a soldier who killed an incapacitated Palestinian attacker, a move criticized by Palestinians and international observers.

items.subject: My decision
bullets: A recent poll shows the North Carolina Senate race is statistically tied, with GOP super PACs spending over $100 million to try to defeat Democrat Roy Cooper and keep Senate control.
Cooper criticizes opponent Michael Whatley for ties to Big Oil, appointing a convicted child sex offender to party leadership, and being President‑backed after Thom Tillis withdrew.
He urges supporters to donate immediately to sustain the grassroots campaign and flip the seat, noting the $100 million GOP dark‑money surge threatens his narrow lead.

items.subject: Republicans Are Suddenly Fighting for Their Lives in Ohio (with Andrew Tobias)
bullets: Ohio, once the nation’s top swing state, has turned solidly red with Trump winning by 11 points in 2024, yet this cycle it’s unexpectedly competitive due to a single dominant local issue.
Signal Ohio reporter Andrew Tobias joins Sarah Longwell to dissect the key players and dynamics shaping the Ohio race, explaining why Republicans now feel their political survival is at stake.
The episode also promotes an upcoming AMA on Oct 2 and offers premium, ad‑free access to the full discussion for subscribers.

items.subject: Here’s the ‘Pathetic’ Reason Trump Is Running His Corrupt ‘Love Me’ Ads
bullets: The White House is airing taxpayer‑funded TV ads, including a “Love Me” spot denouncing “communists,” which watchdogs and Democrats say violate federal anti‑propaganda rules.

GOP operatives describe the campaign as “pathetic,” noting Trump’s massive personal war chest makes the ads unnecessary, yet the administration plans additional ads about a plot against Maduro and a Mount Rushmore PSA.
Officials label the ads “public service announcements,” insisting they are not campaign ads, while critics argue they serve to boost Trump’s image ahead of the 2026 election cycle.

items.subject: “In nature, the poison and the remedy are often found side by side”
bullets: Jonah Weiner recalls a 2010 Rolling Stone contract that paid him $90,000 a year for 35,000 words, a rarity now, and laments how celebrity profiles have shrunk to Q&A and videos, losing depth and craft.

Pascal Baudar, a former tech creative director who lost his fortune in the dot‑com crash, now teaches foraging and wild‑crafted food, showing how poison and remedy coexist in nature and how Michelin‑star chefs use his wild‑clay ceramics to create a “full circle” dining experience.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: When Did Voters Stop Caring About Policy?
bullets: Pfeiffer argues that voters aren’t driven by detailed policy outcomes but by a basic belief that a candidate will improve their personal lives, regardless of specific promises.
He notes Democrats feel punished for focusing on policy, citing Biden’s unrewarded achievements and voters’ willingness to back Trump despite empty rhetoric.
Pfeiffer suggests the next Democratic president will be consumed with undoing Trump-era damage, implying policy relevance remains secondary to perceived personal impact.

items.subject: Trump Shuts Out the Press, ICE Opens Fire, and We Stand with Springfield
bullets: Will Saletan reports Republicans cheering Trump’s ban on White House reporters, while Adrian Carrasquillo details an ICE agent’s fatal shooting in Austin, Texas.
Brendan Hartnett reviews six hours of Trump‑TV programming, and Cathy Young exposes white‑nationalist language surfacing in State Department communications.
The Bulwark’s Dayton event raised nearly $250,000 for the Haitian Support Center after over 1,000 attendees rallied to support Springfield’s Haitian community.

items.subject: Another Day Off
bullets: Krugman announces a brief hiatus, promising a detailed primer on interest rates in his next newsletter.

items.subject: McConnell’s Corpse Casts Deciding Vote on Iran War (w/ Alex Wagner)
bullets: Trump claimed at a state dinner that China is supplying Iran with drone and missile guidance parts used to target U.S. soldiers, prompting Senate Republicans to block a vote to end the war before the midterms.
Alex Wagner’s new book "The Steal" examines the origins of today’s supermajority Supreme Court and warns Republicans may attempt to seize another seat in the lame‑duck Congress.
The episode also discusses how election deniers plan to contest November results and includes Tim Miller’s take on GOP candidates evading responsibility for the Iran war.

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 88: Trump’s White House Press Ban Backfires
bullets: Removal orders for undocumented children doubled under Trump, with over 200,000 orders—70% for kids under 13—driven by Stephen Miller’s deportation push.
A UN legal expert says Trump’s Caribbean and Pacific boat strikes, now killing at least 231 people, violate international law and may constitute crimes against humanity.
A federal judge temporarily blocked Trump’s press ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico, ordering restoration of credentials after the administration cited dubious national‑security claims.

items.subject: Ten Lesbians Walk Into a Bar . . .
bullets: The government allegedly lied to a court again, while JD Vance is accused of leaking national‑security information and Trump is said to have compromat on Susan Collins; Mary Peltola faces a context‑collapse scandal.
JVL apologizes for cutting a promo, and the newsletter highlights a Massachusetts lesbian bar story that was “not woke enough,” calling it a solid B‑/B episode.

The newsletter promotes a Bulwark LIVE tour in October with guests like Bakari Sellers, Pete Buttigieg, and Mark Hertling, and notes that “How to Eat an Elephant” hit #2 on the NYT bestseller list, surpassing Ted Cruz.

items.subject: A Bipartisan Bet on Bringing Movies Back to America
bullets: A bipartisan group of senators and representatives introduced a federal film tax credit offering a 20% credit on payroll compensation, stackable with state incentives and potentially rising to 30% with bonuses for multi‑state spending and disaster‑area shoots.

The credit applies to both above‑the‑line and below‑the‑line wages but excludes profit participation, aiming to keep star salaries taxable in the U.S. and reshore jobs, with Treasury overseeing implementation and no content‑based restrictions.

Paramount’s recent settlement obligates it to spend an additional $1.5 billion in U.S. production over five years, and if the federal credit passes, U.S. production could rise to 20‑30% of its output, or 40% with complementary state credits.

items.subject: A few things that may convince you
bullets: Republican figures including Trump, Vice President Harris, and Stephen Miller are personally targeting Roy Cooper, with GOP spending over $100 million to defeat him in North Carolina.
Cooper says a recent poll shows his narrow lead has shrunk to a statistical tie as GOP super PAC attack ads increase, threatening Democratic Senate chances.
He urges a $7 donation before Wednesday’s fundraising deadline to counter GOP spending, protect his lead, and help flip North Carolina for the Senate.

items.subject: *TICKETS* Join Mehdi for the Premiere of Zeteo’s New AIPAC Documentary in Chicago
bullets: Zeteo and IMEU Policy Project will premiere the investigative documentary ‘Night Flower: Inside AIPAC’s Fight for Influence’ in Chicago on Oct. 20, examining AIPAC’s political sway and election impact.

The post‑screening panel includes Congresswoman Delia Ramirez, Zeteo founder Mehdi Hasan, Pulitzer‑finalist reporter Dion Nissenbaum, IMEU director Margaret DeReus, and commentator Kat Abughazaleh, with a live audience Q&A.

items.subject: You guys are the best.
bullets: The Bulwark team is traveling to Ohio for a live show supporting the Haitian community in Springfield amid Trump administration deportations, with venue size expanding due to high attendance.

Sarah Longwell’s book *How to Eat an Elephant: One Voter at a Time* debuted at #2 on the New York Times bestseller list and stayed there a second week, while readers are actively leaving reviews on Amazon and Goodreads.
An AMA with Longwell is scheduled for Friday, October 2 at 2 p.m. EDT, inviting audience questions about the book and its ideas.

items.subject: The ‘End Times’ Fascists Want Doomsday. Can They Be Stopped?
bullets: Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor argue that a coalition of billionaires, right‑wing politicians, and religious fundamentalists is driving a new era of fascism that threatens ecological and human survival, citing the Trump administration’s Gaza reconstruction plan and ongoing genocide.

They warn that unregulated artificial intelligence could become as toxic as AIPAC money, while centrist leaders like Chuck Schumer enable fascist gains, and propose Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 NYC mayoral campaign as a practical blueprint for resistance.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Why We’re Going to Springfield
bullets: White House finally allowed reporters from Politico, CNN, and MSNOW to enter the complex after a court order, but CNN and MSNOW staff were still denied entry to President Trump’s state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Bill Kristol is hosting a Bulwark LIVE benefit in Dayton to raise money for the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, having already raised $85,000 and selling over a thousand tickets for the event.

items.subject: Two Screenshots, Minutes Apart
bullets: Two Screenshots, Minutes Apart

items.subject: Netanyahu Slams Mamdani and Piker Before Nearly Empty UN
bullets: Netanyahu’s UN General Assembly speech attacked New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and left‑wing streamer Hasan Piker, falsely claiming Piker said “America deserved 9/11” and accusing them of praising Hamas supporters.
Piker responded with a brief, pointed rebuttal, noting he had never endorsed 9/11 and had clarified his remarks in a prior Zeteo interview.
The newsletter also flags bizarre Trump‑linked political ads that may violate taxpayer‑funding rules and mentions ongoing Iran war developments.

items.subject: Don’t boil the ocean: Reach passive positives
bullets: The 2026 fall vaccine rollout is lagging due to limited outreach budgets and public fatigue, so the author urges targeting “passive positives” – people with questions or logistical barriers – rather than trying to reach everyone.

In a recent subscriber webinar, Dr. David Higgins and Dr. Ben Rosenberg identified the size of the passive positive population in the U.S. and offered concrete steps for clinicians, pharmacists, school nurses, community health workers, and public health departments to engage them.
The newsletter includes answers to the top eight audience questions from the webinar, focusing on practical strategies to improve vaccine access for this group.

items.subject: Day Off
bullets: Krugman announces he's taking a day off and will publish a primer on interest rates tomorrow.
He is uncertain whether a podcast will be released tomorrow.

items.subject: The Bulwark’s Cruelest Assignment Yet: 6 Hours of Trump TV
bullets: The Bulwark’s “Cruelest Assignment Yet” has Brendan Hartnett spend six hours watching the new White House “Trump TV” livestream, which loops Trump footage and attracted only a tiny audience.
The episode details the chaos after CNN, Politico and MS NOW were temporarily banned then reinstated at the White House, yet CNN still lacks assurance of re‑entry into the TV pool.
It also critiques right‑wing media’s failed attempt to create its own press pool, citing technical glitches, missing pool protocols, and footage that appears to follow Trump’s motorcade too closely.

items.subject: Trump L’Oil: A Fake Fix for High Diesel Prices
bullets: Diesel prices in the U.S. have surged to near‑record highs, roughly double pre‑Iran‑war levels, hurting truckers, farmers and consumers nationwide.
Trump is reportedly considering a ban on U.S. diesel exports—a move with no precedent that would restrict trade and likely cause economic, diplomatic and political backlash.

items.subject: In Gaza, ‘Whoever Survives the Bombing Won’t Survive the Rubble’
bullets: Amr Adas recounts the collapse of Gaza’s Al‑Saada building, which killed 11 children—including his 6‑year‑old son Bilal and 12‑year‑old daughter Dunya—and ten adults, with dozens injured or missing.
He blames Israel for blocking heavy rescue equipment and forcing families into unsafe, war‑damaged structures due to repeated displacement, bombardment, harsh weather and lack of funds.
The piece warns that over 2,000 Gaza buildings remain at risk of collapse, suggesting many more tragedies like Al‑Saada are likely in the coming weeks and months.

items.subject: Republicans Are Running Out of Gas on Trump’s Iran War
bullets: Republican lawmakers in key House and Senate races are publicly breaking with Trump over the Iran war, citing the national gasoline average of $4.48 and diesel over $6.50 as voter‑pain points.
The Trump administration is flirting with a 90‑day ban on U.S. diesel exports as a short‑term fix, but analysts say it won’t lower prices and Senate Republicans view it as politically untenable.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: No One Should Panic About the NYT Poll in Maine
bullets: The New York Times/Siena poll shows Democrat Abdul El‑Sayed up 5 points in Michigan, Democrat Chris Pappas up 5 points in New Hampshire, but Republican Susan Collins ahead of Troy Jackson by 3 points in Maine.
Collins’ lead threatens Democratic Senate hopes: without Maine, Democrats must win three of Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska—states Trump carried in all three elections—to secure a majority.
Despite the poll, the author argues Democrats shouldn’t panic, suggesting the Maine race isn’t decisive enough to overturn overall Senate prospects.

items.subject: Elon Musk Endorsed Socialist Healthcare Before Campaigning Against It
bullets: Elon Musk’s America PAC is running ads on Roku and door‑knocking in Maine, accusing Senate candidate Troy Jackson of supporting “government‑run” Medicare‑for‑All and labeling him a socialist, while also targeting former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown and former Virginia Congresswoman Elaine Luria with similar claims despite neither supporting Medicare‑for‑All but having backed public health insurance options in the past.

Musk, who once publicly praised government‑run “socialist” healthcare as having majority support, now uses his wealth and platform to attack Democrats and Democratic socialists—Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio‑Cortez, and Zohran Mamdani—by portraying them as endorsing a socialist agenda that would eliminate private health insurance.

items.subject: Our Politicians Suck. But Our Voters Do, Too.
bullets: The newsletter highlights a live fundraiser in Ohio for the Haitian Support Center, praising community support and expressing gratitude for the Bulwark’s impact on listeners.

Janan Ganesh’s Financial Times piece argues that Western leaders are uniformly unpopular, attributing this to voter discontent with necessary reforms and structural issues like partisan sorting, gerrymandering, and democratized primaries.

DraftKings is criticized for abandoning AI tools that could identify problem gamblers, with the company’s responsible gaming division canceling predictive models despite evidence of their effectiveness, mirroring Big Tobacco’s deceptive practices.

items.subject: Bumbling MAGA Media Tries to Launch Their Own White House Pool
bullets: Major networks have stopped using the White House’s official video pool after Trump banned CNN, Politico and MSNOW, leaving a live‑feed void.
Pro‑Trump outlets Real America’s Voice and LindellTV have launched their own White House pool, claiming to provide an "unfeathered" view and offering footage to anyone.
Executive Parker Sigg says the Real America’s Voice pool began after a mysterious late‑night call to cover Trump’s UN visit, though it’s unclear if the White House requested it.

items.subject: This race reminds me of 2016
bullets: Roy Cooper urges $5 donations to his North Carolina Senate campaign, citing his 2016 victory over Governor Pat McCrory by 10,277 votes amid a 0.22% margin and recount controversy.

He claims the current race mirrors 2016, with The New York Times labeling it the best chance nationwide for Democrats to flip a Republican-held Senate seat, and warns that momentum alone won’t secure victory without grassroots support.

Cooper stresses that any margin is fragile, urging donors to prevent Republican opponents and right‑wing super PACs from gaining even an inch, and frames his 2016 win as a result of similar grassroots efforts.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Trump Kowtows to China
bullets: Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, ruled that Trump’s ban of CNN, MSNOW, and Politico from the White House violated constitutionally adequate due process, ordering their reinstatement, yet reporters were still denied entry immediately after the ruling.

Trump’s unprecedented visit to Joint Base Andrews to personally greet Chinese President Xi Jinping, mirroring a similar 2025 visit for Russian President Putin, was a symbolic gesture of deference that is unlikely to yield substantive policy changes, especially on China’s stance toward Iran and regional aggression.

The article critiques Trump’s pattern of appeasing authoritarian leaders—highlighting his minimal references to democracy and human rights in a UN speech, his praise of Putin’s child‑repatriation efforts, and his overall strategy of avoiding confrontation with Russia and China to protect his political base.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: 40 Days Out: Democrats Have the Edge in Both Chambers
bullets: With just 40 days until Election Day, Democrats hold a statistical edge in both the House and Senate according to recent polling and race analyses.
Former President Trump’s approval among Republicans has fallen below 50%, a sharp drop from the ~70% levels seen in 2018, 2020, and 2024, weakening GOP turnout prospects.
Pfeiffer promises ongoing, detailed updates on key House and Senate contests to cut through the flood of ads, polls, and misinformation.

items.subject: EXCLUSIVE: Poll Finds Even Most Republicans Want U.S. to Investigate Israeli Killings of Americans
bullets: A bipartisan Senate resolution led by 24 Democrats, including Sanders and Warren, would force the State Department to report on nine Americans killed in the West Bank since 2022 and on Palestinian children’s detention, with a vote possible before the October recess

Exclusive Data for Progress polling shows a supermajority of likely voters, both Democrats and Republicans, support investigating these killings and the broader Israeli violence in the occupied West Bank

items.subject: Donald the Deadbeat Does Diesel
bullets: Trump is likely to impose a U.S. diesel export ban to lower domestic prices, but economists say it would only temporarily help Texas while raising diesel and heating‑oil costs elsewhere, including the Northeast and West Coast, and could also lift gasoline prices by curbing refinery output.

The ban would breach contracts with energy firms and damage trust with allies, signaling that the U.S. cannot be relied on as a stable fossil‑fuel supplier and undermining its geopolitical competition with China’s clean‑energy push.
Politically, the move reflects GOP desperation as the party faces a probable midterm loss, and it would further expose Trump’s pattern of broken promises and opportunistic policy swings.

items.subject: Andrew Weissmann Just Won a BIG Free-Speech Victory
bullets: CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued the Trump White House after he barred them from the press pool, alleging illegal suppression of news coverage.
A federal court ruled in favor of Andrew Weissmann, dismissing Cassidy Hutchinson’s former lawyer’s defamation claim against him.
Paramount settled a states’ antitrust suit over its Warner Bros. acquisition, ending a major media consolidation challenge.

items.subject: Here’s How Trump’s White House Press Ban Hurts MAGA Media Too
bullets: The White House’s ad‑hoc “national security” ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico was struck down in court, with a judge likely ordering the outlets’ access restored on due‑process grounds.

Trump’s press ban, intended to curb critical coverage, backfired by harming right‑wing media; the ban’s reversal is now crucial for the MAGA media landscape to regain White House access and influence.

items.subject: Dems’ Newest Campaign Line: Trump’s Gonna Freeze You to Death
bullets: Democrats are using rising heating‑oil prices to warn voters that winter costs will spike, blaming Trump’s Iran policy for the surge in petroleum‑dependent energy costs.
The campaign message frames the heat wave and winter chill as a political issue, suggesting Republicans will face higher heating bills if Trump’s policies continue.

items.subject: Here’s How the Left Can Defeat the Fascists
bullets: Varoufakis argues fascism rises when capitalism faces crisis and the left offers no credible alternative, warning that fascists will co-opt anti‑capitalist rhetoric but ultimately ally with big business and finance to consolidate power and expand militarism.

He calls for an anti‑fascist economics built on three pillars: state‑directed investment, banning private banks from creating money, and instituting one‑employee‑one‑share‑one‑vote corporate governance to restore worker control and shared prosperity.

items.subject: Portrait of an Anti-Anti-Trumper in Despair
bullets: Gerard Baker, former WSJ editor, published an essay claiming Trump’s policies caused inflation, deficits, and a “reckless military adventure” that disrupted global energy, but downplays Trump’s authoritarian actions.

The author of the brief criticizes Baker’s portrayal, labeling it cowardly and arguing that Trump’s real threats include a secret police, support for dictators, and the Jan. 6 attack on constitutional order.
He warns against treating former anti‑Trump defenders like Baker as allies, urging vigilance toward anyone shifting away from Trump without genuine commitment to liberal democracy.

items.subject: She’s Gen Z. She’s an Immigrant. And She’s Going to Congress!
bullets: Melat Kiros, a Gen‑Z immigrant, won Colorado’s Democratic primary against a 15‑term incumbent and is poised to become the first Gen‑Z woman in Congress, promising to shake up establishment politics.

She says democratic socialism is needed to curb billionaire‑driven AI tech and will likely back Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker while holding Twitch streamer Hasan Piker to higher accountability than many officials.

items.subject: This Is a Five-Alarm Fire for Medical Research
bullets: The Trump administration is reportedly drafting an executive order that would require political officials, not just scientists, to approve NIH grant applications, threatening the agency’s $50 billion budget where 80% funds external research.
Policy analyst Russell Vought, a key Trump ally, is pushing the plan and has already pressured NIH by canceling grants, demanding a 40% budget cut, and targeting DEI‑related projects.
Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have blocked the proposal in a stopgap spending bill, and NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya has publicly opposed the politicization of grant reviews.

items.subject: Take it from me, this is close
bullets: Roy Cooper’s North Carolina campaign is in a tighter race than expected, with his lead cut in half since Trump’s super PAC began buying ads, and the GOP’s $125 million war chest is flooding the airwaves.
The state’s large, dispersed electorate makes advertising expensive, forcing Cooper’s team to rely heavily on donations to counter the GOP’s financial advantage and protect voting rights.
The author urges immediate $5+ contributions to help Cooper’s campaign fight back against the super PAC’s spending and secure victory before Election Day.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: We Watched Six Hours of Trump TV
